newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kinshasa says ex-Mobutu troops in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa says ex-Mobutu troops in Brazzaville.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's government on Thursday accused both sides fighting across the river in the Congo Republic's capital Brazzaville of hiring mercenaries from the defeated army of ousted Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko.
It threatened "military measures" if Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo becomes the target of fresh provocations or shots landing in the capital Kinshasa.

Deputy Interior minister Faustin Munene told journalists that the ex-government troops had fired shells from across the river Congo into Kinshasa since fighting broke out on June 5 in Brazzaville between the army and ethnic or political militia.
Kabila's government has threatened to retaliate before.
Munene said President Pascal Lissouba's government was against Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire throughout its campaign to oust Mobutu.

"Both sides are using mercenaries from the Mobutu DSP (Special Presidential Division). This conflict is fishy. Both Lissouba and the other (Lissouba's rival, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso) are using Zairean forces as mercenaries. That's our concern," Munene said.
"If they keep up with acts of provocation, we will react in self-defence. We are in a state-of-law. If they provoke again, so much the worse for them," he said.
He said plots were under way in Brazzaville against Kabila's government. He declined to elaborate on who was involved.
Munene suggested that shooting in Brazzaville on Wednesday night had triggered a "wind of panic" in neighbouring Kinshasa.
Soldiers of the Alliance forces fired several shots into the air in different districts of Kinshasa following a resumption of shooting in Brazzaville on Wednesday night.
"I went out in the street myself. I was driving around in order to find out what was going on. One of my body guards was hit (by a bullet from Brazzaville)," he said.
"If this repeats itself, we will take military measures. We don't want the panic to go on," he added. He gave no details.
Brazzaville residents said the shooting there appeared to be a celebration at progress in restoring peace rather than a breach of a truce.

Kabila seized power in May, after a bush war. Hundreds of soldiers of Mobutu's defeated army crossed the river to Brazzaville as Kabila's forces triumphantly entered Kinshasa, following Mobutu's flight into exile.
Brazzaville is less than three km (two miles) from Kinshasa.
Other members of Mobutu's defeated army have been sent to Kitona, 400 km (300 miles) south-west of Kinshasa, for training before joining a national army that is taking shape.
Munene acknowledged that there had been "difficulties" in Kitona between Kabila's soldiers and the ex-government troops but denied that there had been a revolt.
